4.0.s.en: 1. His asking Job's permission to speak

4.0.0.en: 1 Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: 2 "If one test a word with thee, wilt thou be offended? But who can refrain from speaking?

4.0.2.en: This introduction reveals that the three friends had conferred together and agreed to confront Job in a serious manner, for they supposed that he had deceived them and the people by the piety, worship and giving to others that he displayed. And that his outward appearance hid secret evils that no one knows but God.

4.0.3.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem says that Eliphaz spoke to Job without shame, in an unbecoming spirit, as one who wished to overthrow this firm, strong and established tower. He observed that Job opened his mouth (Job 3:1), while Eliphaz answered (Job 4:1). The first spoke in innocence; he opened his mouth to utter words so that he might find in his friends comfort for what had befallen him; but Eliphaz answered as one who carried within him, he and his friends, a bitter struggle, desiring to crush him. Eliphaz's words came as an answer to questions in his own soul and a revolt within him!

4.0.4.en: If one test a word with thee, wilt thou be offended?

4.1.0.en: But who can refrain from speaking! [2]

4.1.1.en: It seems that the friends, despite their silence, carried within them a suppressed boiling in their hearts. They look at Job on the dunghill not with eyes of pity but with intense vexation that he had deceived them and all those around him; but the deception could not last, for God exposed him for his evils and his deceit.

4.1.2.en: When Job opened his mouth and murmured, they supposed that he had gone far beyond bounds, and they could keep silent no longer. They had endured him all week while he was silent, and had endured his deception. Now that he has murmured and cursed the day of his birth they regard themselves as men of God, defenders of God's justice and righteousness!

4.1.3.en: They supposed that Job's murmuring and his questions contained an insult to God's justice, so they had to answer his questions firmly.

4.1.4.en: He begins his speech by saying: If someone examines the matter and speaks to you a frank word, will you be offended? But even if you are offended, we cannot keep silent. He seems, like one in politeness and modesty, to ask permission for everyone to speak with him. And frankly he tells him that, although they feel his pains, they cannot flatter or cajole him. Perhaps Eliphaz wanted to ask Job not to misunderstand them and think that they are harsh with him, or that they do not care about what he suffers; they do not wish to add sorrows to his sorrows, but to find the right door for remedying the situation.

4.1.5.en: * By the words he utters, Eliphaz strikes as with a trumpet to proclaim war against Job.

4.1.6.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem *Not everyone is able to know how to minister to those in such trials. Many often add pains to pain, some through baseness, others through folly.

4.1.7.en: It is clear that those who undertook to offer words of comfort were inexperienced in this matter, like physicians who increase wounds. Therefore they rightly deserved to be called by Job evil physicians (cf. Job 13:4), those who inflamed the wound out of the spite within them.

4.1.8.en: It is a kind of baseness to show spite with a violent outburst, and to envy a man who was cast down on the ground, and to throw him into countless difficulties, one who deserved to be treated with gentleness.

4.1.9.en: Observe how their words were not only devoid of comfort but caused grave discouragement. They stirred up long discussions with renewed accusations.. Hence it was said: [Add not more troubles to a distressed heart] (Sir 4:3).

4.1.10.en: St. John Chrysostom The Septuagint reads: "Wilt thou speak much in grief?" St. John Chrysostom sees that "grief" here means "sin," as if he were saying to him: [Under thy tongue is toil and pain] (cf. Ps 10:7).

4.1.11.en: *Eliphaz did not say: Do you commit evil deeds? but said: "Will you speak?" because the fame of his life was radiant throughout the length and breadth of the earth, for everywhere there were testimonies to his virtue. He did not say to him: Do not say that your works are good, for sin sometimes springs from words.

4.1.12.en: *"Who can bear the violence of thy words?" (Septuagint)... What did Job say? He besought death and deliverance from the present life. Did he say: "So many evils have overtaken me despite my righteousness and my great virtues"? No, but he said this: I long to disappear with the wicked, with my servants, with the stillborn, that I may obtain the same as the wicked obtained. He did not say: I, who have such traits and such importance.

4.2.0.en: 3 Behold, thou hast instructed many, and hast strengthened slack hands. 4 Thy words have raised up him that stumbled, and thou hast established the trembling knees!

4.2.1.en: Eliphaz began by praising Job for his teaching, his guidance and his giving to many, and he had to begin thus, because Job's practical life bears witness to this. On the one hand he wanted to show that he is a just man who does not distort reality, and on the other he wanted to use this praise to attack Job as a vain man.

4.2.2.en: At any rate, Eliphaz's words revealed to us Job's character as a living leader who bears a spirit of fatherhood in his concern to guide many, and in his generosity in giving.

4.2.3.en: Behold, thou hast instructed many, and hast strengthened slack hands [3].

4.2.4.en: He praises him as a practical teacher and guide, for he taught many and strengthened the slack hands so that they might work and serve. But he is as one saying to him: If you strengthened others with your wealth, why can you not strengthen yourself?

4.2.5.en: * Let us contemplate the towering height the man attained by guiding the ignorant, supporting the weak, and strengthening the slack, and this amid the cares of his house, his many obligations, his anxiety for his children, and the oversight of many affairs; for he had devoted himself to setting others on the straight path. But all heretics and wicked men, when they record the loftiness of the good, turn this loftiness into accusations.. Thus (Eliphaz) seeks an opportunity to revile the blessed Job from the very angle from which he recounts things praised in him.

4.2.7.en: Thanks be to Eliphaz who, though out of malice and not out of love, presented to us a wonderful aspect of Job's character. For as a king or ruler or chief of a tribe he was not a man who loved authority, commanding and forbidding, but in fatherhood he guided, advised and strengthened the slack hands.

4.2.8.en: For there are many guides, but they do not support the weak, nor do they bear a spirit of fatherhood. St. Paul says: "For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor 15:4). The true spiritual guide bears the spirit of truth, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of love, of whom the Lord Christ says: "Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth" (Jn 13:16). He who bears the spirit of truth offers practical help along with guidance, strengthening the slack hands, as the Apostle says: "comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 14:5).

4.2.9.en: St. Augustine sees that this is the way of him who offers the remedy to the citizens of the city of God during their journey on earth, that the Holy Spirit may work, granting healing to the sick souls so that they may enjoy reaching the heavenly homeland.

4.2.10.en: * If we hate the wicked and the disobedient, then we hate sinners. Thus, consequently, you will find that you have cut yourself off from most of your brethren, in truth from all, for there is no one without sin.

4.2.11.en: If we must hate the enemies of God as worse than ravening beasts, then we shall scorn everyone and swell with pride like the Pharisee.

4.2.12.en: Paul commands us otherwise: "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14).

4.2.13.en: *"Though ye have ten thousand instructors... yet have ye not many fathers" (1 Cor 15:4)... Paul does not seek any honor here, but rather shows the depth of his love. Honor belongs to the instructor, and love is the mark of the father.

4.3.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Thy words have raised up him that stumbled, and thou hast established the trembling knees [4].

4.3.1.en: How much Job strengthened the slack hands for fitting work, took the hands of the stumbling and raised them from the dust, and strengthened their knees to bear them to walk in the way of life by the power of God. So Eliphaz praised him, so that when he rebuked him Job might not think that he was prejudiced against him, or ignoring his past with all its good deeds. Job comforted many, so he deserves to find one who comforts him.

4.3.2.en: Some commentators see that Eliphaz mentioned this to rebuke Job, as if saying to him:

4.3.3.en: [You who guided many, why do you not guide yourself?

4.3.4.en: And you strengthened slack hands, why did you not find rest for your weakness?

4.3.5.en: And if you helped the stumbling with words, why are you cast down on the ground in your body as in your soul?

4.3.6.en: If you established the trembling knees, why did you not encourage yourself, but are broken down before the diseases that have come upon you, walking as though paralyzed?

4.3.7.en: Is this not proof of your hypocrisy, that you offer the medicine to others and refuse to receive it yourself for healing of your sickness? You who taught others not to break down, do you break down? "Physician, heal thyself" (Lk 4:23).

4.3.8.en: See, your former talk was perhaps vain, and the good that you did contains folly!]

4.3.9.en: * Our neglect of our brethren is no light fault, but brings upon us great punishment and chastisement without mercy...

4.3.10.en: Persistent counsel and teaching make a man diligent and bring him to a better state, and in this I cite the common proverb that confirms this truth, that "constant drops of water split the rock."

4.3.11.en: What is softer than water?! And what is harder than rock?! Yet persistence in work continually overcomes nature. If this is so with nature, shall not human nature all the more be overcome...?!

4.3.12.en: What a large part of the body of the Church resembles the dead, without movement!!

4.3.13.en: You say: And what concerns us in this?

4.3.14.en: You have a very great capacity with regard to your brethren. For you are responsible if you do not counsel them, and ward off evil from them, and draw them here with power, and pull them out of their extreme slackness. For is it fitting for a man to be profitable to himself alone, and not profitable to himself and to many as well?

4.3.15.en: The Lord Christ made this clear when He called us [salt] (Mt 5:13), and "leaven" (Mt 13:33), and [light] (Mt 5:14), for these things are useful and beneficial to others.

4.3.16.en: For the lamp does not shine for itself but for those sitting in darkness. And you are a lamp, not to enjoy the light alone, but to bring back a man who has gone astray; for what benefit is a Christian who does not benefit others?! and who does not bring anyone back to virtue?!

4.3.17.en: Again, salt does not season itself but seasons food lest it spoil and perish... So God has made you spiritual salt, to bind together the corrupt members, that is, the lazy, slack brethren, and to strengthen them and rescue them from sloth as from corruption, and to bind them with the rest of the body of the Church.

4.3.18.en: And this is the reason why the Lord called us "leaven," for leaven too does not leaven itself, but though small it leavens the whole lump, however great. So do you also. For though you are few in number, be many and strong in faith and zeal toward God. And as leaven is not weak because of its smallness, since it has power and capacity by its nature... so you can, if you wish, draw to yourselves greater numbers than you, and they will have the same level of zeal...

4.3.19.en: For this reason do not gather here in vain. Rather I do not cease to beseech you with all zeal, as I used to do before, saying: "Come here with your brethren. Guide here. Guide the erring. Teach them by deeds, not by words only"...

4.3.20.en: May the God of peace and love, who removes from our spirits all rancor, bitterness and anger, condescend and grant us - through our being joined to one another in perfect unity as the members are joined to one another (Eph 4:16) - to offer Him with one accord, one mouth and one spirit the praise of our due thanksgiving.

4.3.21.en: St. John Chrysostom If we ignore Eliphaz's intention, we find a living testimony to a godly man who did not belong to Isaac the son of Abraham, a king and not a priest of any people, and yet he set in his godly heart the support of the stumbling and the strengthening of the trembling knees. He will judge many of God's servants and priests in the Old Testament as in the New. For there is no pastoral work greater than bending down toward those fallen to the ground to take their hands and rise with them. If the divine Word became incarnate and came down to our earth in humility, and carried us in Himself up to heaven, so it befits every servant, indeed every believer, to support and help so that all may enjoy fellowship with God.

4.3.22.en: By setting forth Job's traits, Eliphaz presented us with a living method of pastoral care, indeed of the life of faith, and of how every believer cares for the life of his brother through love, without ignoring his concern for the salvation of his own soul and the salvation of his household.

4.4.s.en: 3. His rebuke for his lack of steadfastness

4.4.0.en: 5 But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. 6 Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways?

4.4.1.en: But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest!

4.4.2.en: It toucheth thee, and thou art troubled! [5]

4.4.3.en: Eliphaz rebukes Job, saying to him that when his turn came to drink the cup of affliction he collapsed, fainted and was terrified. Here begins the attack to accuse him of hypocrisy. As if he were saying to him: When you were in prosperity you taught well, but when you fell into what others fall into, your weakness was exposed and your patience ran out.

4.4.4.en: * Minds fond of disputation attack the lives of the righteous in two ways: either by asserting that what they utter is wrong, or that they utter the truth which they do not observe in their conduct. Thus the blessed Job was rebuked by his friends over his manner of speaking. They encourage him because he speaks true things, but he does not keep them himself... Observe how they first praised him for his tongue, then complained of the weakness of his life. For the wicked, so as not to show themselves as wicked, sometimes say good things about the righteous, knowing that others know this about them.

4.4.6.en: St. John Chrysostom justifies Job's distress and behavior, for it is a natural reaction to the multitude and severity of the calamities and the suddenness of their occurrence, besides the behavior of his friends and their provocative accusations against him.

4.4.7.en: We cannot ignore that it befits the leader, being in the position of leader, guide and father, not to be quickly disturbed before trials, so as to be a secret of strength and comfort for others.

4.4.8.en: * No one does more harm to the Church than those who have the appearance and title of holiness yet behave corruptly. And it is a grave error to entrust the place of pastoral care to a deficient person, since pastoral care is an example. A wrong choice of shepherd results in grave consequences, for while in sin he receives honor on account of the position he has taken. Let every unworthy man flee from the weight of this great iniquity and ponder, listening with the ears of his heart to this voice that says: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Mt 18:6; Lk 17:2). Here the millstone signifies the whirlpool of life, and the depth of the sea points to eternal perdition. It is far better that a lay person who by himself put on the garment of holiness in outward show should perish alone than that this man should put on himself the garment of pastoral care and destroy others by his wicked example. And I am sure that the punishment of hell will be lighter if this man falls into it alone without being the cause of others' falling with him.

4.4.10.en: * Although a man may keep himself pure from sin, even in lofty degrees, yet I know that one in this condition cannot lead others to virtue. For he who has received the care of a people, it is not enough for him to be free of sin... but he must rise in doing good, as the commandment says: "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27).

4.4.11.en: So he must not only have the traces of vice wiped from his spirit, but also be furnished with virtues, so that he may surpass them in virtue rather more than his loftiness over them in honor.

4.4.12.en: He must know no limits to doing good or to spiritual growth, nor think it a great gain merely to excel over ordinary people.

4.4.13.en: He must not measure himself against others, whether wicked or somewhat advanced spiritually, but measure himself by the light of the commandments. Nor should he measure virtue on a small scale, since it flows from God the Greater, for "of him, and through him, and to him, are all things" (Rom 11:36).

4.5.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways? [6]

4.5.1.en: Here he rebukes him for the piety he showed during his prosperity: where is this piety? And where is your hope and the uprightness of your way? Are not all these vain pretensions with no roots in your depths?

4.5.2.en: Eliphaz carried out Satan's work and served his interests, for he wanted to stir Job up to blaspheme God by accusing him of hypocrisy, and that this piety, hope and uprightness of his were all vain appearances.

4.5.3.en: *"Is not thy piety founded on folly, and also thy hope and the perfection of thy way?" (LXX) By this he seeks to distort his former virtuous deeds... He is stabbing at Job's intention while he works. He means either that you did not work, or that your life is full of deceit, or that you did not fear God with an upright intention, but it was all mere talk. Your hope is without reason, it is full of folly... If your deeds were sincere and your life pure, you would not fear these evils...

4.5.4.en: You see how Eliphaz attacks him, wrestles with him, and makes every effort to prove that his folly brought these troubles upon him...

4.5.5.en: "By the commandments of the Lord they are destroyed" (9 LXX). Observe another thing.. He says: Do not think that demons and wicked men full of spite are responsible for what has befallen you. For God is chastening you, therefore the chastening is just, beyond dispute.

4.5.6.en: St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase: [Where is your fear (piety), your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?] that although he reviled him unjustly, he described precisely the ordering of the virtues and their ladder or degrees, which are the fear of the Lord, then trust in God, then patience, and finally the attainment of perfection:

4.5.7.en: a. The fear of the Lord, or piety, is the beginning of the way. "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence" (Prov 14:26).

4.5.8.en: * Let us not count wealth a very good thing; for the great good is not to possess money, but to acquire the fear of the Lord and all the paths of godliness.

4.5.9.en: * Fear is no less than a wall, a protection and a mighty tower.

4.5.10.en: St. John Chrysostom b. Through the fear of the Lord we pass to strength, or "strong confidence in God," which appears only in trial.

4.5.11.en: * The fear of the Lord contains all those requirements (for continual joy). For the man who fears the Lord as is fitting, and trusts in Him, gathers all the sources of happiness and acquires the perfect fountain of delight. Just as a drop of water falling into a wide ocean quickly vanishes, so whatever befalls him who fears the Lord is dissipated and vanishes in the vast ocean of joy.

4.5.12.en: It is truly most wonderful that, even with causes of sorrow present, you find the man rejoicing. For since there is nothing at all that brings sorrow, this bitterness is of no value to him compared with his enjoyment of continual joy.

4.5.13.en: St. John Chrysostom c. Through trust in the Lord the believer enjoys patience. For a man is approved, in the true sense of the word, and grows in strength by bearing the faults of others. He who cannot face his opponent is wounded by the sword of cowardice.

4.5.14.en: * For four days we have been occupied in explaining the parable of Lazarus (and the rich man), presenting the treasure we find in a body covered with sores. A treasure not of gold and silver, but of wisdom and endurance, of patience and forbearance.

4.5.15.en: St. John Chrysostom d. Patience leads to perfection. For a man is truly perfect when he is long-suffering toward the weaknesses of others. [In your patience possess ye your souls] (Lk 21:19).

4.5.16.en: This is the ladder of perfection: the fear of the Lord and piety toward Him give us confidence in Him, and this gives us strength amid trials, this strength gives us patience in bearing others with their weaknesses, and by this patience we reach the ways of perfection.

4.5.17.en: * There are two forms of perfection, an ordinary one and a higher. One is acquired here, the other hereafter. One is according to human capacities, the other belongs to the perfection of the world to come; but God is just through all, wise above all, perfect in all.

4.5.18.en: St. Ambrose * The Apostle speaks of himself as perfect and imperfect. He counts himself imperfect, looking at how much righteousness he still lacks, yet perfect in that he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and that he is advancing to attain perfection.

4.6.0.en: 7 Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? 8 Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. 9 By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed. 10 The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. 11 The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad.

4.6.1.en: Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? [7]

4.6.2.en: Eliphaz presents a practical proof of the accusation he directed at him. For - in Eliphaz's opinion - no righteous man has perished, and no upright man has been destroyed. He asks him for a single example, from Job's long experience throughout his whole life, of a righteous or upright man who suffered what Job has suffered.

4.6.3.en: This is a theological, moral principle that prevailed in many minds, for even after the Law David was astonished, reproaching the Lord, how the way of the wicked prospers and He allows afflictions to the righteous. But he soon discovers the truth, for the righteous will surely receive their heavenly reward, and the wicked who persist in their evil will fall under judgment. The Psalmist says: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb... I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found... But the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD: he is their strength in the time of trouble" (Ps 37).

4.6.4.en: Eliphaz's speech is true if by perishing and destruction he meant what is eternal, but to apply it to temporal calamities is not correct. Therefore his speech does not apply to Job, for he had not perished eternally.

4.6.5.en: The prophet says: "The righteous perisheth" (Isa 57:1). And the Wise Man says: "There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked" (Eccl 9:2), until temporal life ends and on the day of the Lord this one is separated from that.

4.6.6.en: * [What innocent man perishes? and where do the upright perish?] But it often happens in this life that the innocent perishes and the upright are utterly destroyed, yet in their perishing they are kept for eternal glory. If no innocent man perished, the prophet would not have said: "The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart" (Isa 57:1). If God in His providence did not destroy the upright, Wisdom would not have said of the righteous: [Yea, quickly was he taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding] (Wis 4:11).

4.6.8.en: * The wicked, unbelieving man, even if we suppose that he wraps himself in a heavenly body, remains naked because he does nothing to obtain the garment of the inner man.

4.6.9.en: St. Didymus the Blind * How beneficial are the trials and sufferings which some consider evil! The saints do not try to avoid them, but truly seek them with all their strength, enduring them courageously, and thus become friends of God, and obtain the crown of eternal life... And the blessed Apostle exults, saying: [I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong] (2 Cor 12:10).

4.7.0.en: Father Theodore Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity and sow wickedness reap the same [8].

4.7.1.en: Eliphaz relies in his arguments on two main factors: his personal experience and observations: "as I have seen" [8], and "visions of the night" [13 etc.].

4.7.2.en: Eliphaz thought that through his observations he was presenting an exact theory, for he found through his statistics that calamities befall the wicked in proportion to their wickedness, that is, justly; but Job refuted this theory (Job 17:21 etc.).

4.7.3.en: It seems that Eliphaz did not react to the severity of the affliction that had befallen Job, and supposed that what befell him were light pains proportionate to his hidden wickedness, while his grave evil was his excess in murmuring against God.

4.7.4.en: Thus Eliphaz was hoping that Job would repent of his hidden evils so that the afflictions would be removed from him; but his cursing the day of his birth, this is what utterly crushes him!

4.7.5.en: This is fulfilled daily, for "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (b), as the Apostle Paul wrote: "Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you" (2 Thess 1:6). And it is said: "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword" (Rev 13:10). But God in His longsuffering waits for the repentance of the wicked, and in His love allows affliction to the righteous so that they may be approved.

4.7.6.en: Job's friends were pressing him, those who had come to comfort him! And like enemies they were troubling him with bitter words.

4.7.7.en: * The only comfort for those who find themselves in misery and grief is to be cleared of guilt, lest they appear to have borne their pains and misfortunes as punishment for sin. But his friends seemed to be trying to take away even this comfort from the holy Job, so that he would appear to be the cause of his own misery, as one who brought down the Lord's wrath by his grave iniquities, and that he endures these afflictions as the price of his wicked deeds! And they described the punishments of the wicked (cf. Job 8:4-9), who planted vices and reaped sorrows for themselves! These perished at God's command, for they were consumed by the breath of His wrath, which blew upon those dwelling in houses of clay, and they withered (cf. Job 19:4, 21) LXX, and God frustrates the plans of the crafty and shuts the mouth of the wicked (cf. Job 13:5, 16) LXX; and what the friends alleged was true as regards the power of the Lord, but untrue as regards the merits of that great righteous man.

4.8.0.en: St. Ambrose By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed [9].

4.8.1.en: All that the wicked devise and plan perishes by a breath from God, and all their wicked schemes fail. This is true: God is longsuffering with the wicked as He was longsuffering with Pharaoh of Egypt in the days of Moses the prophet, but when the cup of their evil is full He destroys them, that the rod of the wicked may not rest upon the righteous; so He destroyed Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea. This does not apply to Job, because what befell him was for his approval and not for his destruction.

4.8.2.en: Eliphaz wanted to terrify Job that the bitter calamities that had befallen him were only the beginning, and that if he did not confess his hidden evils and put away his pride, his fate would be destruction and annihilation.

4.8.3.en: *(As if Eliphaz accuses him thus:) You are not as you suppose yourself to be in your pride, for you seek by deceit to make others consider you so. See what you have really done, as is plain from the corruption of your body. Your offspring also perished, and the best of your wealth, and all your property, and the crown of your inheritance. For in truth you are not pure, and in truth it is as you suppose. What a sick man you are in this matter... for it is not unjustly and without cause that these calamities have swallowed you up, but they are in harmony with justice, since God aimed them at you.

4.8.4.en: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem At any rate, if both the righteous and the wicked are exposed to trials and afflictions, the soul of the former exults within him amid the sufferings because he receives the afflictions from the hands of God for his purification and approval. But the wicked groans within, and finds himself as one fallen into a net, and he may examine himself and return to the Lord his Savior, or may persist in folly and distress in his evil, and so fall into bitterness in this world as in the age to come.

4.8.5.en: *"The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth" (Ps 5:11)... He approves His righteous by testing them, but the wicked He hates. His soul loathes the wicked who love injustice...

4.8.6.en: He is the Judge of the righteous and the wicked; the wicked are judged because by their love of injustice they hate themselves... And as Solomon says in Proverbs: "He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul" (Prov 32:15). If he who loves injustice despises himself, then he who loves righteousness loves himself; and this agrees with the proverb: [He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul] (cf. Prov 8:19)...

4.8.7.en: "Upon the wicked he shall rain snares" (Ps 6:11). Without doubt, for it is the Lord who sets snares for the sinners themselves, to catch those who have corrupted their freedom and must walk the straight way under His bridle, so He gives them the possibility of advancing through Him who said: "I am the way" (Jn 6:14).

4.8.8.en: *"How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" (Ps 1:84), in which a man's dwelling is changed from earth to heaven... The mind and heart filled with longing for the Lord's dwelling are fruitful and happy! When death comes upon the sinner, his thought is found occupied not with this dwelling but with punishments. He does not meditate on the Kingdom of Heaven, but on the terror of the flames of hell.

4.8.9.en: * [The ungodly are like the dust which the wind driveth away] (Ps 4:1). Scripture says that the wicked man will be wretched, not even like the dust of the earth. For dust seems to have no being, yet it surely has a kind of existence in itself... It is scattered here and there and has no single place, but the wind sweeps it away, and it has no power to resist. The same is true of the wicked. As soon as he denies God, the breath of Satan sweeps him away in error and throws him wherever it wishes.

4.8.10.en: * Wretched is the man who has masks of evil, and happy is the man who has many masks of goodness.

4.9.0.en: St. Jerome The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken [10].

4.10.0.en: He likens the unjust and cruel persecutors to roaring, howling lions. Through divine justice the sound of their roaring ceases, and their voice no longer terrifies in the wilderness or the forests. And their teeth are broken so that they cannot tear, that is, God takes their weapons from them, and they are no longer able to prey [11], so they die of hunger and leave no cubs to succeed them.

4.10.1.en: Perhaps Eliphaz wanted to accuse Job indirectly, declaring to him that he had been like a ravening lion, with none in the region who could stand before his might. His words were like the roar of the fearful lion, plundering and devouring in injustice and tyranny. But behold his might has vanished, his wealth is scattered and his family is lost, and not one son is left him like a cub to occupy his place.

4.10.2.en: Thus Eliphaz turned from praise to blame.

4.10.3.en: The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad [11].

4.10.4.en: *It is easier for a lion to be cowardly than for the righteous man to walk an easy life.

4.10.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Eliphaz compares Job to a lion because of his kingly power, but he rightly adds: "the roar of the lioness" (Septuagint), alluding to the greatness of Job's virtue. He also added "the arrogance of dragons" since he wished to speak of his spirit, calling this beast (the dragon) king among reptiles. At any rate Eliphaz says that all this is broken; it tramples on the sufferings of the righteous...

4.11.s.en: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

4.11.0.en: 12 "Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur thereof. 13 In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, 14 fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook. 15 Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. 16 It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof: an image was before mine eyes. I heard a low voice: 17 Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? 18 Behold, he putteth no trust in his servants, and his angels he chargeth with folly: 19 how much more them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, and who are crushed like the moth? 20 Between morning and evening they are destroyed. Without any regarding them they perish for ever. 21 Is not their tent-cord plucked up from them? They die without wisdom."

4.11.1.en: Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur (a whisper) thereof [12].

4.11.2.en: Here Eliphaz relates to Job a vision he saw, presenting it in order to condemn him. Some see that God gave Eliphaz this vision to calm his soul when he heard what had befallen Job. And that he saw this vision before meeting the tried Job.

4.11.3.en: This vision was presented to him secretly as a word that stole to him, like one whispering in his ears.

4.11.4.en: In humility Eliphaz confessed that he had received a small portion of the divine mystery and had not grasped the whole vision as he ought.

4.12.0.en: In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men [13].

4.12.1.en: In the middle of the night, when people were still and fell into deep sleep, that is, slept, Eliphaz was preoccupied with what lay behind what happened to Job, so God showed him this vision. The Psalmist David invites us to speak in our hearts with God, and to be silent until God speaks with us: "Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still" (Ps 4:4). And as St. Mar Isaac the Syrian says: "Let your mouth be silent, and your heart will speak; and let your heart be silent, and God will speak."

4.12.2.en: It befits us at night to remember God and meditate on His law, and He will reveal to us His secrets and wisdom. "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches" (Ps 63:6).

4.13.0.en: Fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook [14].

4.13.1.en: It seems that before seeing the vision he felt a trembling shake all his bones. His heart was filled with the fear of the Lord, and he realized His greatness and felt that he was too small to reproach God. Thus he was prepared to receive the divine message. The Psalmist urges us: "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling" (Ps 2:11).

4.13.2.en: Then a spirit passed before my face.

4.14.0.en: The hair of my flesh stood up [15].

4.14.1.en: A spirit passed by Eliphaz, most likely an angel sent from God, to serve the Word. And the hair of his skin stood up, for the heavenly beings have been an object of terror to man since Adam's fall; he fears that a painful message will reach him and does not expect good news.

4.14.2.en: In ancient times the Levites were obliged to shave all the hair of their bodies (Num 8:6-7), since it represents unnecessary bodily matters. So Eliphaz, bearing evil toward Job, could not bear the spirit passing before his face; he lost his peace and his whole being was disturbed until the hair of his body stood up, a sign of the fullness of his disturbance even regarding what is superfluous in his body.

4.14.3.en: It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof.

4.15.0.en: An image was before mine eyes [16].

4.15.1.en: Eliphaz saw the angel clearly; he passed before him as an apparition, "an image before mine eyes," or as one who sees in a mirror, unable to describe him: "I could not discern the form thereof."

4.15.2.en: The voice came to him softly, for we do not hear the quiet voice of God amid the noise. Elijah did not meet God in the tempest, but in the quiet, gentle breeze (1 Kgs 19:11-13).

4.15.3.en: Eliphaz bore bitter carnal thoughts toward Job, therefore when the spirit passed by him he could not with his carnal mind see spiritual things, but saw what was more like phantoms, and could not distinguish the voice of the Spirit, which was low; his ears could not distinguish it. Thus Eliphaz confessed without knowing it that he had lost his peace, so the visions of the night became troubling imaginations. He could not sleep and rest while men were sleeping in deep sleep. His bones trembled, the hair of his body stood up, and his mind was confused with phantoms. This is the fruit of the corrupt man who turns truth into falsehood and slanders his brethren unjustly.

4.16.0.en: Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? [17]

4.16.1.en: The message came to rebuke Job for his murmuring; he does not dare claim to be more righteous than God, nor purer than He.

4.16.2.en: "Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?" (Isa 45:9).

4.16.3.en: "Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee" (Jer 1:12).

4.16.4.en: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 2:143).

4.16.5.en: "Let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged" (Rom 4:3).

4.16.6.en: "Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight" (Rom 20:3).

4.16.7.en: * For a man to be righteous he must keep the Law in everything, which human nature can hardly accomplish. Since every man is a liar, on that day when the Lord comes to judge mankind, He alone is justified in what He says, for His words are true in everything, they are words of truth.

4.16.8.en: Origen * I do not trust in myself, but I ask for the mercies of Thy truth and justice. "Enter not into judgment with thy servant" (Ps 2:143). How clearly the prophet declares his confidence in the tenderness of Christ, when he says: [Summon not thy servant to judgment before thee].

4.16.9.en: St. Jerome * If every man is a liar, and God alone is truth, what befits us, the servants of God and His bishops, but to cast away human errors and obey the Lord's commandments?

4.17.0.en: St. Cyprian the Martyr Behold, he putteth no trust in his servants, and his angels he chargeth with folly [18].

4.17.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that he is speaking here of the heavenly powers, for God does not trust them, in the sense that their nature is not immune from error.

4.17.2.en: St. Basil says in his letter to Amphilochius that the heavenly powers have freedom of will and can incline to good or to evil, therefore they need the Spirit's help.

4.17.3.en: As he says in his third treatise against Eunomius that the authorities and principalities, etc., have holiness from their striving and continual contemplation of God, and are not holy by their own nature, and that, as they long for goodness, they receive holiness according to the degree of their pure love for God.

4.17.4.en: And in his treatise on the Trinity he says that these heavenly beings derive holiness from the Holy Spirit according to the rank of each. Thus it appears that they are not good by nature, but by the freedom that draws them to goodness and grace.

4.17.5.en: What keeps the angels from falling now is that their contemplation of God grows and increases, and secondly their awareness of the trial that befell the fallen angelic orders on account of their pride, this together with their continual resistance to the wicked angels increases their longing for goodness and their approval before God.

4.17.6.en: * The lilies represent the radiant beauty of the heavenly angels, whom God clothed with the splendor of His glory. They neither toiled nor spun, for they received from the beginning what they always are. And since at the resurrection men become like the angels, He wished us to hope for the beauty of the heavenly garment, so that we may be like the angels in splendor.

4.17.7.en: St. Hilary * Truly men and angels are accounted harsh if compared with You, for You alone are the King of all tenderness... We ask that You be the Judge, for You are tender toward all nations!

4.17.8.en: St. Jerome * The nature of an angel is rational, intelligent and free, subject to change, that is, of changeable will. For every created being is changeable, and only the uncreated does not change. And everything rational is free. Since its nature is rational and intelligent it is free, and since it is created it is changeable, having the capacity to remain and advance in goodness, and to turn to evil... And the angel is immortal not by nature but by grace.

4.17.9.en: Father John of Damascus It seems that the following statements are not part of the vision, but are Eliphaz's comment.
